title: Three Aspects of Consciousness
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of cultivating awareness and presence in our daily lives through meditation practice. By letting go of preconceptions and simply paying attention to our surroundings, we can experience moments of contentment and joy even in chaotic situations. This practice allows us to deepen our emotional lives, become more open and appreciative of others, and ultimately transcend the limitations of our individual selves, revealing a deeper connection to ourselves and the world around us.

sentences.text: Well, some of you I know were here yesterday and I was talking about the point of meditation, what we're trying to do.
Today I want to talk a little bit more about meditation practice in its wider sense.
I'm going to use a framework of three aspects of consciousness.
I'm getting this framework from a great book, which I recommend to everybody, by Dale Wright, about the six paramitas.
Dale Wright is a Zen scholar and practitioner who writes with great intelligence and thoroughness.
I've been reading his book for a long time, over and over again, so a lot of what I'm saying depends on his thinking.
We're living in a scientific age, so we have to pay attention to science; it yields a lot of truth.
According to science and also according to Buddhism, every living being has some kind of consciousness.
Science studies the material world, so it holds that consciousness is somehow an emergent quality from matter.
Consciousness is associated with matter; there isn't any independent consciousness.
And as far as I know, Buddhist thought says the same thing.
Actually it was one of the Buddha's key points, and he differed in this from pre-existing Indian thought.
It was one of his key points that there is no independent self-existing consciousness apart from the physical world.
As far as I'm aware, Buddha didn't explain what consciousness is.
When he was asked to do things like that, he said, "That's not my problem, I'm not interested in that.
I'm only interested in how consciousness functions in our lives."
Also, science doesn't know what consciousness is either.
Just like the Buddha, science studies consciousness through its effects in the material world, because science studies physical objects, like the brain.
But of course consciousness is not like some secretion inside the brain.
And consciousness is not an object, so science cannot study consciousness since it's not an object.
So, in conclusion, maybe we have no idea what consciousness is.
Maybe we'll never know; maybe it's impossible for us to know what it is.
Even though our entire lives unfold at the heart of consciousness, and even though consciousness is the most important thing, we may never know what it is.
In fact, according to some schools of Buddhism, consciousness is not only the most important thing, consciousness is the only thing.
So, as I said, in science all living beings have consciousness.

But in Far East Asian Buddhism, which is where our Buddhism comes from, not only do all living beings have consciousness, but even rocks and trees and roof tiles also have consciousness, as Dogen is so fond of saying.
But anyway, if pebbles have consciousness, for sure animals and other living things have consciousness.
Plants probably have some kind of consciousness too.
Different sorts of beings have different sorts of consciousness.
And I'm saying beings have consciousness, but the word "have" is highly misleading.
But we have to say something.
So let's say, and this is where I'm drawing now on Dale Wright, that human beings have three kinds of consciousness.
The first kind we could call immediacy, or immediate consciousness.
This is our basic sense of being embedded in a world.
We have perceptions: we see, we hear, we taste and so on.
You don't have to think about seeing something in order to see something.
You don't have to think about hearing in order to hear.
You might not want to hear, but if there's a loud sound, you hear it anyway.

Whether you think it, whether you want it, we will see and hear and taste and so on, because this is the way our sense organs work and this is the way the physical world interacts with our sense organs.
When a sense organ cognizes a sense object, consciousness arises and we're aware of what we hear or see.
And this already is, how did that happen?
It's already a miracle.
It's a strange thing.
How could that be?
And yet, there it is.
Nobody knows exactly how that happens.
Then, as we know, right away when we have a cognition, a perception, we have a feeling.
Immediately.
We have an immediate feeling, and our reactions to things are immediate.
We like it.
We don't like it.
Immediately.
We're frightened by it.
It makes us happy immediately.
Even before we know what it is, even before we've had a chance to think it over, boom, we have a reaction right away.
So this is also part of our immediate consciousness.
Then sometimes we have dreams, in half awake, or visions, that we see things that aren't there.
That happens.
It probably happened more in the past than it does in the present, although now people can take drugs and so on and have visions.
But in the past, probably people were walking along minding their own business and always seeing Buddhas and bodhisattvas and dragons and demons.
Where do you think all those dragons from the myths came from?
They saw them.
And these are also immediate consciousness.
These things just come to us.
We don't ask for a dream or produce it somehow.
It just happens.
Then also we can have a memory.
It just happens.
It's immediate.
Pictures from our life.
Sensations.
Things we simply feel and know about our lives.
Feelings about all that, immediately coming up in our life.
All of this that I'm describing, many things, this is just immediate consciousness.
It's natural and normal.
We don't think about it.
We don't reflect about it.
We don't produce it.
So much of our lives are like this: immediate and simply given, without any effort on our part.
Any desire.
Any strategizing.
Boom.
The whole life appears.
Now I think that for human beings even language is a part of our immediate awareness.
We don't have to make a tree be a tree, or ponder a tree.
As soon as we see a tree, it's a tree.
We know it's a tree.
Probably somewhere buried deep in our mind is the word "tree."
That gives us the experience of a tree even though it's quite immediate.
And if somehow we had no language at all, I think we would have a very different kind of immediate experience in our lives.
Our lives would be quite different.
Radically different if we had no language at all.
So images and words, it seems to me, are part of the immediacy of our consciousness.
So that's one level of consciousness that I think we can all understand.
We might wonder about the details of it.
I'm not sure about the details of it.
Somehow we know we do have immediate experience of our lives and of the world.
But then we also have a second kind of consciousness: reflective consciousness.
We have the ability to think about things.
We can have immediate experiences but then we step back and we can reflect on those experiences.
We can evaluate them.
We can make decisions about our lives based on our evaluations and our thinking.
And then we can create elaborate stories about our lives and about other people's lives.
We can make whole novels in serial, one novel after another.
We can make giant feature films with sequels that we're creating about what we think is going on in our lives.
So in other words, that's an elaboration based on our immediate reactions and experiences.
And then we can have much more elaborate emotional lives based on those novels and stories that are very different from our immediate visceral emotions.
And we create huge edifices of abstraction that we call the world.
There's no world or society.
There's no society.
We've created this incredible abstraction that's effective, and things happen because of these abstractions.
And then we have various thoughts and theories.
You read the newspaper and there are huge thoughts and theories about society and government and what's going on and so on and so on.
An incredible thing that we've created based on our immediate experience.
The whole world of the 21st century is a product of reflective consciousness, right?
Nations.
When people first conceived the idea of nations, it was a revelation.
It was a big abstraction: we're a nation.
And then we have nations, we have governments, we have economies.
None of this could exist without reflective consciousness.
So this is a serious thing, reflective consciousness.
It has a big impact on everything, and we spend a lot of time on this aspect of our lives.
It's very important.
It's what makes our lives so complex and so rich and also so tragic.
And it's the way we shape our lives.
We live our lives based on our reflective consciousness.
We build a life with reflective consciousness.
We have rational thinking, critical thinking.
We can change the world in big ways.
We can change our lives in big ways.
Probably our reflective consciousness is the big thing that characterizes our humanity.
I'm sure other animals have immediate consciousness that is more or less the same as ours and probably far more wonderful than ours in so many ways that we don't even understand.
We'll never know.
Animals probably have a very rich life of immediacy.
But other animals don't seem to have this kind of complex reflective consciousness that we have, fully elaborated by our many forms of language.
So many other animals make houses, and it's pretty amazing the kind of houses that they make.
But no other animal would have constructed New York City.
You can't imagine, like beavers getting together and building New York City.
It's not possible.
Even though a beaver dam is an impressive thing.
So this is what happens when there's reflective consciousness.
At one time we thought this is why we're superior to other animals.
I think now we're getting the clue that this probably doesn't make us superior.
It has its advantages and its disadvantages.
Anyway, at least we can say it makes us different.
At least it appears that it makes us different, at least from some point of view.
So that's reflective consciousness.
Now we're on the third consciousness: self-consciousness.
Very strange.
Very strange form of consciousness.
It basically comes down to the fact that in the middle of all this stuff, here I am.
I'm a person experiencing a life.
So in other words, the world is not just happening randomly, a bunch of stuff.
The world is happening to me and to you.
Every one of us is actually the center around which the entire world is swirling.
So first, to review: this immediate experience; then there's reflective consciousness, thinking and shaping the experience.
And now here we are, the third kind of consciousness: being a person experiencing all this.
The person who's doing the thinking and the reflecting, who's perceiving this immediate world.
Now this one, this third one, is really weird, because built into the middle of it is a very powerful and probably painful paradox.
None of us can actually experience ourselves the way we can experience a sensation or a perception or a thought.
The one who knows is incapable of directly experiencing the one who knows.
In Buddhism, the way they say this is: a fingertip can't touch itself.
It's true, right?
This fingertip, there's no way that this fingertip could touch itself.
And they say the eye can't see itself.
So you might immediately say, "Yeah, well, that's cute.
But I don't need to touch my fingertip, because I can touch it with the other fingertip.
So what's the big deal?"
Or, "I can look in the mirror and I can see my eye.
I can take a picture of my eye and I can look at it."
But it's not the same thing.
In the mirror or in the photo, you see the image of your eye, not the eye.
And when you touch your fingertip with the other fingertip, you're touching an object.
You're not experiencing a fingertip as a fingertip from the inside.
A fingertip cannot touch itself.
An eye cannot see itself.
A subject perceives an object but can never perceive the subject itself.
You can have a thought about yourself, but you cannot directly experience yourself, because any experience, any perception requires that there be an object.
And you are exactly not an object.
So even though we are very sure that we are ourselves, we can never experience ourselves directly.
Just like you can never actually see yourself.
Even in the mirror, even in the photograph, you are not seeing yourself.
You're only seeing reflections.
You're only seeing objects that stand for ourself but they are not ourself.
You can either be happy or sad to realize that nobody looks like the photo.
Right?
You don't look like the photo.
Not really.
And anyway, even if you did look like the photo, your outward form is not really you entirely, right?
It's only some shapes and colors and so on.
So who notices this?
We don't even think about this.
We don't notice it.
But the truth is that self-consciousness is very bizarre, very strange, and inherently very painful.
Because everybody knows, we all know, as Descartes said, I know already.
I'm thinking, therefore I know I must be here.
So we know we're here.
We know we're ourselves.
We know we are definitely here at the center of our lives.
We know that each one of us is the organizing principle.
If there's an organizing principle of your life, what is it?
You.
You are the organizing principle of your life.
Even that phrase, your life, my life, already, there are leaps involved in that conception.
But we know we're definitely here.
And everybody, whether they're smart or stupid, knows that they're here.
And yet, no matter how smart you are or stupid, you don't know yourself.
You can't.
You can only see your effects in the world, and you can only see pictures of yourself, never your actual self.
So our actual self, and this is like a stunning thing to think about, our actual self is like a person we love a lot, whom we'll never meet, who we long for our entire lives and will never meet.
And that is something beautiful and strange and slightly disturbing.
Don't you think?
Now, I apologize.
I'm not here to theorize about consciousness.
The reason why I'm putting all that out is because now I want to say, how does meditation practice influence us in these three realms?
So now that's what I want to talk about.
So first, immediate experience.
As I indicated, immediate experience really is quite miraculous.
Just to be able to see and hear and experience objects of the world is a profound and wonderful thing.
As we all know, because we've all felt this ourselves, almost all of us feel sometimes lonely, depressed, confused, unfulfilled, unhappy, misunderstood.
But really, it's hard to see how anyone could feel that way in the middle of such an extraordinarily beautiful and amazing world.
The world is so powerful, how could anybody ever be unhappy?
I mean, you look up in the sky, the depth of the sky, unbelievable, the sun so far away, and yet warming us up.
It's the immediate experience of the sun 93 million miles away.
So lovely.
The rain, it's a miracle, so refreshing.
The snowflakes today, amazing.
Babies are born.
You look at them, you're like staggering, staggering.
Plants are growing.
Nobody makes them grow.
I used to be a farmer, I would always be amazed.
Look at them, they're coming up, a whole field of them.
So in this world, what else could anybody need?
What else could anybody need but just being in this world?
Even unpleasant sensations are wonderful.
Even though our reactions to them can be quite painful, but even so, the fact that these reactions are impacting consciousness and vividly bringing life to bear is somewhat immense.
And all of our immediate experiences are like that, miraculous, wonderful.
And there is really no good reason why simply being alive in a world like this shouldn't make us feel grateful and happy all the time.
There's really no good reason for it.
But who feels that?
Nobody feels that, right?
Even though we know it's true and it makes sense to us, nobody feels that.
Why?
Because we're usually not able to experience the immediate world with its full impact, right?
We just assume that the world is there, fine, and we barely notice.
Why?
Our minds are full of all the worries that we have, all the vague, dissatisfied thoughts and feelings that some of them come to consciousness, but most of them are roiling around under there darkly.
All of our plans about how we're going to do this and how we're going to do that and how we better do this and we better do that and how the things we better accomplish or who are we.
Or, on the other hand, our various escape routes or all the bad things that probably will happen to us and we better watch out for this and we better watch out for that.
Our minds are completely colonized by all of these thoughts, most of which we're not even aware are there.
And they literally crowd out the immediacy of perception.
And they absorb so much energy that we don't even notice the world around us.
And this is something that I've always found particularly wonderful about meditation practice.

Because you sit there long enough, and usually it takes a while, but you sit there long enough just paying attention to the breath, just returning awareness to the breath, returning awareness to the body, and little by little by little the energy of perception returns to you.
And you can see and feel and hear and taste the world with more joy.
I hope that in our little retreat you've already had such a moment when all of a sudden you just feel content and happy for absolutely no reason other than somebody just put food in your bowl.
And it's lovely to watch them so carefully put the food in your bowl.
That's enough for a whole lifetime.
You're happy.
Even though the world still is crazy, and you still have all the problems you had before, but now you're happy because of this moment.
And that is a wonderful effect of meditation practice.
Just to experience that, just a little bit, redeems one's life.
So when we're in a meditation retreat, we're trying to develop a certain amount of concentration.
We're training the mind to be concentrated in one point.
We bring the mind back all the time to the breath and the body or whatever other theme we might be focusing on.
So there's an effort here that we're trying to do, a gentle but persistent effort.
But that's just one of the ways we're practicing.
Doing that helps us to practice in other ways.
For instance, we are practicing in a retreat like the one we're doing this weekend, a wider focused meditation.
When we're sitting, yes, it's just breath and body and presence and whatever comes and goes in the mind.
It's pretty narrow focus.
But also, all day long when we get up and do the various things we're doing, we practice with a wider focus.
Just paying attention to whatever's there, not just the breath, but whatever appears.
Whatever comes into awareness, we pay attention to that.
So when we're working, we're paying attention to the task.
When we're eating, we're paying attention to the food, how the food looks, how it tastes, texture, smell.
We're paying attention to seeing, to hearing, to touching.
We're just noticing everything that comes into awareness.
Now, I want to say, this is very important, that the practice here is not to become an expert crackerjack noticer.
That's not the point.
I remember one time, very early in my Zen practice, many, many decades ago, I was with a senior student who had been practicing much longer than me at the time.
And we were standing on one side of the street, and somebody that we knew passed on the other side of the street.
And I didn't notice the person, and he noticed the person.
He said to me, "Oh, you're not such a great Zen student, are you?
You didn't notice that other person across the street."
And I thought to myself, even in my naive early days of Zen practice, "That doesn't sound right.
That doesn't sound right.
Zen practice is about whether or not you notice a person on the street?
That's Zen practice?
Or even a thought in my own mind?
That's Zen practice?"
I don't think so.
In other words, being present, being conscious, is not a sport or a contest.
It's simply being willing to be alive, whatever being alive might happen to look like at that time and place.
If this were not the case, then Zen masters would get worse and worse and worse the older they get.
But supposedly, anyway, Zen masters don't get worse and worse.
They get better and better the older they get, even though it's very clear that they are becoming less and less competent the older they get.
So in other words, as their competency goes down, their Zen goes up, which tells you that our practice must be about something other than competency.
So being present is being present with whatever we notice or don't notice.
Being present means letting things come and go, regardless of our level of competency.
And when we are willing to let things come and go, whatever comes and goes, then we can rest in the immediacy of our experience that will come alive with our practice.
So meditation, in other words, what I'm saying here, is meditation actually returns the world to us.
It's not like we have alienated ourselves from the world.
Meditation returns the world to us and returns us to the world.
And this is something that the Zen masters of ancient times appreciated a lot.
And they were always talking about the miracle of perception.
Click, pebble hits a bamboo, and like the world ends.
Wind through the trees, and they're ecstatic forever.
The world wakes us up from our self-obsession and our unhappiness.
And the Zen teachers of old taught us that.
So that's Zen practice in the immediate world.
That could be enough.
That could be enough of a reason right there to practice Zen.
And also meditation practice influences us on the reflective level of consciousness too.

Because now we're not just talking about the sitting practice per se, but about how we think about our lives, how we conceive of our lives, how we speak and relate to other people, how we make decisions.
And if you practice meditation, there's always a context.

Eventually you can't avoid hearing about the Four Noble Truths and all the things that somebody was telling me.
They read like a hundred Vipassana books and they all say the same thing.
Right.
Of course they do.

If you meditate, you're going to hear the teachings.
You're going to hear about compassion.
You're going to hear about precepts.
You're going to hear about all this stuff.
And that's going to influence the way you live your life and look at your life.
That plus the meditation practice that gives you a greater capacity to look at your own life.
And you're going to feel your life differently.
And it's going to dawn on you, inevitably: "Yeah, you know what?

I get to be miserable.

Relationships are better.
When I act with compassion, I feel more love for the world, for myself.
Life is more meaningful.
When I have a path, I'm happier."
We don't have to be the wisest person in the world.
We don't have to know everything every minute to feel that we have a way of life that we know we can trust by our own investigation over time.
So yeah, there's a relationship between our awareness, which is strengthened by our meditation, and the teachings.
We confirm the teachings through our own living.
And this changes the way we think about our lives.
The stories we've been telling ourselves for such a long, long time about who we are and what has happened to us, begin to be revised.
We begin to see that much more is possible than we thought was possible.
We begin to have a new basis for the choices that we make in our lives.
And everything changes, little by little, including and perhaps especially the nature and the quality of our relationships.
I was saying before that we have immediate emotions, but also we have elaborate emotional lives based on our reflective thinking.
And over the time of our practice, as we reflect on the teachings, our emotional life will change.
We will actually feel different emotions, and we will feel the same emotions differently.
We all think of our emotional lives as given.
It just happens.
This is the way I am.
She said this.
Of course I got angry.
But actually, our emotions don't just happen.
We have been training ourselves for a long time to feel our lives the way we have been feeling them.
Little by little, as we practice, we train ourselves differently.
And practice is really, in large measure, a question of cultivating our emotional life.
We feel everything we feel more deeply, more beautifully, more poignantly.

As we get unhooked from our very narrow, very crabbed sense of self-centeredness, we are just more and more open to other people and more and more appreciative of them, even if they are crazy and weird, even more so.
Wow, what a crazy, weird, wonderful human being.
Better not hang around with that one, but still.
But maybe the most amazing part of meditation practice, the most profound effect that it has on us, is on this third level.
Certainly the most mysterious of meditation's effects are on this third level, self-consciousness.
Something, as I said, particular to human beings, it seems.
And you can see it if you look into a pair of human eyes.
They say the eyes are the window to the soul, which is very wise, like so many old sayings.
It's very true.
Now, I'm sure everybody has done this, had a moment when you stared into the eyes of a cat or a dog, possibly a horse, maybe a cow, probably not a pig, because pigs don't sit still for that.

Maybe you see also calmness, maybe you see also neediness, weariness, but on top of all of that, you're going to see something else, something different.
You're going to see human consciousness, the human soul.
You'll see it in those eyes.
And since you also have a human soul, you will see in this other human soul something more than an object.
You will see yourself, your own soul, reflected.
You will see the miraculous wonder of human relationship.
You will see soul meeting soul.
And even if, as it happens in our lives, we can't fully express that needing, you will see its potential.

Unlike everything else we experience, we cannot experience the soul as an object, even though it is mysteriously and fundamentally important to us, maybe the most important thing.
The only inkling we have of it is in the gaze of the luminous presence of another person, where we'll vaguely sense, although we can't grasp, the immensity of it.

So when we feel, as we often do, a deep, gnawing dissatisfaction, or a despair, or a terrible fear that we can't even name, even though sometimes we pin it on something, it doesn't have to do with something that we're lacking, some protection that we need.
